register.name: North Dakota Legislative Branch - North Dakota Century Code (North Dakota Legislative Council)
register.access_notes: Fully accessible. Plain HTTPS GET with the honest user agent 'canon-index-builder/1.0 (+https://github.com/legalese/canon)' worked with no challenge, no rate limiting and no block. Structure discovered by probing: /cencode/tNN.html is a per-title chapter index (chapter number, chapter name, and a '[Repealed]' marker where applicable) and /cencode/tNNcCC.html is a per-chapter section index; the actual statute text is served only as /cencode/tNNcCC.pdf, which was deliberately never downloaded. Titles with a decimal use a hyphen in the path (Title 26.1 is /cencode/t26-1.html; /cencode/t261.html is a 404), and decimal chapters likewise (Chapter 54-52.4 is /cencode/t54c52-4.html). Note that /cencode/ itself returns a ~46 MB response; it was not retrieved beyond a HEAD-style size check. About 30 requests in total, spaced 2 s apart. Verification used only the register's own chapter and section index pages plus the Century Code landing page and the site's disclaimer page.

licence.summary: The register carries no terms of use and no permission or reuse statement. Its only legal page is a bare accuracy disclaimer, and the footer renders a script-generated site-wide notice 'Copyright (c) <current year> North Dakota Legislative Council' - a blanket website notice, not a claim over the statutory text and not accompanied by any restriction on reproduction or adaptation. Under the government edicts doctrine confirmed in Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, 590 U.S. 255 (2020), the text, numbering and section headings of the Century Code, being the work of legislators acting in their legislative capacity, are not subject to copyright at all, so reuse and adaptation are lawful notwithstanding the footer notice. The Century Code here is published by the Legislative Council itself, not by a commercial publisher under contract, and the site states its version is the official one. Treated as open: reuse and adaptation permitted.

register.name: Oklahoma Legislature - Oklahoma Statutes (Oklahoma State Legislature, oklegislature.gov)
register.access_notes: PARTIALLY accessible - read carefully. The Oklahoma Legislature's own site worked over plain HTTPS GET with the honest user agent 'canon-index-builder/1.0 (+https://github.com/legalese/canon)'; no challenge, no rate limiting, about 25 requests spaced 2 s apart. Two significant limitations. (1) The judicial branch's OSCN statute browser (www.oscn.net and oscn.net, 65.71.189.80), which is the usual section-by-section official Oklahoma statute interface, refused all connections on port 443 from this environment (ECONNREFUSED from the agent fetch tool, timeout from curl, 3 attempts); no workaround was attempted. (2) On oklegislature.gov the Statutes are served ONLY as whole-title documents - https://www.oklegislature.gov/OK_Statutes/CompleteTitles/osNN.pdf (plus .doc and .rtf) - which are statute text and were therefore deliberately never downloaded. There is no per-title or per-chapter HTML table of contents: /OSSTATUESTITLE.HTML links straight to the PDFs, /osStatuesTitle.aspx is an ASP.NET postback form, and the CompleteTitles/ directory listing (which was read) contains only osNN and ocNN files with no TOC files. Verification therefore rests on two register-native sources: the official titles index at /OSSTATUESTITLE.HTML for title numbers, title names and the currency date, and the Legislature's own full-text statute search at https://search.oklegislature.gov/query-statutes.php (a GET form taking Title and SearchText), used to confirm that each Act's short title appears in the current statutes of the expected title and to obtain the section numbers that carry it. That search returns citations and a result count but no section catchlines and no per-section status flag, so section-level headings could not be read and are not asserted. A DATE DISCREPANCY WITHIN THE REGISTER: /OSSTATUESTITLE.HTML states 'The Oklahoma Constitution and Oklahoma Statutes were last updated on November 18th, 2025.' while /tsrs_os_oc.aspx on the same site states the same thing 'on October 4th, 2024'; a human should establish which feeds the search index.

licence.summary: The register asserts nothing. No copyright notice, terms of use, disclaimer or reuse restriction appears anywhere on the Oklahoma Legislature site: the titles index, the homepage and the statute search page were each read in full and contain no 'copyright' string and no (c) symbol, and there is no terms or privacy page (/terms.aspx, /privacy.aspx and /about.aspx all redirect away). Under the government edicts doctrine confirmed in Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, 590 U.S. 255 (2020), the text, numbering and section headings of the Oklahoma Statutes are not subject to copyright in any event, so reuse and adaptation are lawful. The Legislature publishes these files itself rather than through a commercial publisher, although a separately copyrighted annotated edition (Oklahoma Statutes Annotated, Thomson Reuters/West) exists whose annotations, notes and index are not part of this material. Treated as open: reuse and adaptation permitted. Caveat for a human: because no terms page exists, the finding is an absence of any assertion rather than an affirmative grant.
licence.attribution: none required and none offered by the register; good practice is to cite 'Oklahoma Statutes' with the title and section and the register's currency date

Every TCP connection to the Oregon Legislative Assembly's hosts was refused or timed out on port 443: www.oregonlegislature.gov and oregonlegislature.gov (205.143.225.10), olis.oregonlegislature.gov (205.143.225.20), api.oregonlegislature.gov, and the Secretary of State's secure.sos.state.or.us. The agent fetch tool reported ECONNREFUSED immediately and curl with the honest user agent 'canon-index-builder/1.0 (+https://github.com/legalese/canon)' timed out after about 22 s, so the failure is at the network layer rather than an HTTP response, and it covers the whole 205.143.225.0/24 block. By contrast www.oregon.gov (a different netblock) answered with a 302, which shows general egress works and the block is specific to these hosts. 6 attempts in total, spaced 2 s apart, retried once after roughly 25 minutes; identical result each time. Per the access rules no workaround was attempted. No chapter title, ORS edition year, in-force status or copyright page could be read, so the acts list is deliberately empty. Public.Law, Justia and Casetext copies of the ORS were not used, because the instructions forbid relying on a secondary site for in-force status.

licence.summary: UNVERIFIED - the register's own copyright page could not be reached at all. This one needs a human look more than the others, because Oregon is the state with the best-known history of asserting copyright in its statutes: the Legislative Counsel Committee claimed copyright in the ORS (over the numbering, headings, tables, index and annotations that Legislative Counsel adds, rather than the enacted text) and pursued that claim before backing down in 2008 after the Public.Resource.Org dispute. The ORS is published by the Legislative Counsel Committee rather than by a commercial publisher. As a matter of US law the enacted statutory text is not copyrightable under the government edicts doctrine confirmed in Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, 590 U.S. 255 (2020), and that decision also reaches the headings and numbering where they are produced under legislative authority - but what the site asserts today, and in what words, must be read from https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/Pages/ORS.aspx and the Legislative Counsel copyright notice before this is relied on. open_licence is set to false as a conservative default meaning 'not established', not as a finding that reuse is prohibited.
